doc.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022

title: Lower Manhattan arts scene and Ornette's Lonely Woman
summary: How he learned jazz terminology in 1960s lower Manhattan among artists; Ornette played him Lonely Woman. Roommate painter Bob Thompson, pick-up basketball and bars with poets and painters.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I love the way you combine adjectives and nouns which — I’ll give you an example, at the end of “Dear John Coltrane” and you said, “If you, J.C. and Bach ever swap infinite fours” I just think that’s marvelous, like “infinite fours.” And it also begs the question how did you learn about the terminology that jazz musicians use all the time? The trading of fours, and the exchanges and back and forth? Was that by observing or did someone sort of take you under their wing and talk to you about that?

Well in New York I knew a lot of jazz musicians and I knew them very well. I mean that was a part of our world. The thing about the lower Manhattan arts scene in the 1960s was about as close as America ever got to say Montmartre at the turn of the 19th and 20th century, the modernism there. A great concentration of artists of all disciplines living in a relatively small area. They all knew each other, they all hung out together, they went to each other’s parties, they drank together, and the exchange was wonderful. And lower Manhattan at that time you could drop in on people like Ornette Coleman or Alan Ginsburg or Larry Rivers, sit down and have a drink and watch them work and they’d talk to you. And I went by Ornette’s once and I remember he said, “A.B. I’ve got this new tune, I think it’s going to be really good. I’ve got some problems to work out over here in this part of it, but I think once I get that set up it’s going to be really good and let me play for you what I’ve got so far.” And it turned out to be “Lonely Woman” which I © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

think was one of Ornette’s greatest, greatest tunes. You’d go by, I was roommates with a painter named Bob Thompson who is getting some attention right now, and Bob, he’s been dead for several years. And he’d be there working and he’d be there working and have his music on. That’s one, painters could listen to jazz and work. I always envied that. They’d have it up really, really loud and he’d be practically dancing into his canvas and he’d be talking about it. And it’s the same with all the musicians, I mean you’d be playing basketball at a pick-up basketball game at Tompkins Square Park and you’d be playing with poets and painters and actors, you know, and it’s just a pick-up game but it’s also exchange. You see what I’m saying? Then of course there are the bars which we all went to more than we should have. So yeah, so I knew a lot of jazz musicians, and once I started writing about it they would seek me out and they’d have new records and “Can you write my liner notes for me” you know. “Can you put me on your radio” — I had a radio show on WBAI for a while. “Can you play this record on the radio show?” So I got to know them, and I would go to their recording sessions sometimes and so you know I got to look into the music quite a bit and got to hear them speak. And so yeah, I learned all this stuff from them. They taught me how to write about music, or how to write about them basically.
